claim: Current xenogeneic mouse models cannot evaluate on-target off-tumor adverse effects due to limited human/mouse cross-reactivity of antibodies used in CAR and severe graft-versus-host disease induced by administered human T cells.
source: Current xenogeneic mouse models cannot evaluate on-target off-tumor adverse effect, hindering the development of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapies for solid tumors, due to limited human/mouse cross-reactivity of antibodies used in CAR and sever graft-versus-host disease induced by administered human T cells.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a limitation of current models, drawing on established knowledge about xenogeneic model limitations.

claim: GPC1-specific human CAR-T cells showed strong antitumor effects in xenogeneic mouse models.
source: GPC1-specific human and murine CAR-T cells generated from our original anti-human/mouse GPC1 antibody showed strong antitumor effects in xenogeneic and syngeneic mouse models, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically Figure 2E showing tumor growth inhibition.

claim: GPC1-specific murine CAR-T cells showed strong antitumor effects in syngeneic mouse models.
source: GPC1-specific human and murine CAR-T cells generated from our original anti-human/mouse GPC1 antibody showed strong antitumor effects in xenogeneic and syngeneic mouse models, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figures 4E, 4F, and 4G showing tumor growth inhibition and complete tumor eradication.

claim: Murine GPC1-specific CAR-T cells enhanced endogenous T cell responses against a non-GPC1 tumor antigen through the mechanism of antigen-spreading.
source: Importantly, the murine CAR-T cells enhanced endogenous T cell responses against a non-GPC1 tumor antigen through the mechanism of antigen-spreading and showed synergistic antitumor effects with anti-PD-1 antibody without any adverse effects in syngeneic models.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 4J and 4K showing gp70-specific IFNγ production and tumor rejection upon re-challenge.

claim: GPC1-specific CAR-T cells showed synergistic antitumor effects with anti-PD-1 antibody without any adverse effects in syngeneic models.
source: Importantly, the murine CAR-T cells enhanced endogenous T cell responses against a non-GPC1 tumor antigen through the mechanism of antigen-spreading and showed synergistic antitumor effects with anti-PD-1 antibody without any adverse effects in syngeneic models.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6C and 6D showing enhanced tumor control with combination therapy.

claim: CAR-T cell therapies have demonstrated robust clinical responses in hematological malignancies.
source: Immunotherapies with a chimeric antigen receptor T (CAR-T) cells have been demonstrated robust clinical responses in hematological malignancies.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in the field, supported by the citation context (June et al., 2018).

claim: Development of CAR-T cell therapies for solid tumors has met several obstacles including on-target off-tumor lethal toxicities, insufficient activation of administered CAR-T cells in tumor tissues, and loss of target antigens in tumor cells.
source: However, developments of CAR-T cell therapies for solid tumors have met several obstacles including on-target off-tumor lethal toxicities, insufficient activation of administered CAR-T cells in tumor tissues, and loss of target antigens in tumor cells (June et al., 2018; Kato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature documenting these challenges.

claim: Even weak expression of target antigen on normal tissues caused lethal toxicities in the first-in-human clinical trial.
source: For example, even weak expression of target antigen on normal tissues caused lethal toxicities in the first-in-human clinical trial (Morgan et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific clinical trial report.

claim: Most preclinical studies for CAR-T cell therapies have been performed in vivo using xenogeneic mouse models.
source: Majority of preclinical studies for CAR-T cell therapies have been performed in vivo using xenogeneic mouse models wherein response of human T cells against human xenografted tumors are tested (Li et al., 2017; Shiina et al., 2016; Carpenito et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple preclinical studies using xenogeneic models.

claim: Preclinical studies of CAR-T cell therapies in xenogeneic mouse model could not predict the lethal toxicities that occurred in the first-in-human clinical trial of HER2-specific CAR-T cells.
source: Indeed, preclinical studies of CAR-T cell therapies in xenogeneic mouse model could not predict the lethal toxicities that occurred in the first-in-human clinical trial of HER2-specific CAR-T cells (Morgan et al., 2010; Zhao et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations comparing preclinical and clinical outcomes.

claim: Syngeneic mouse models enable analyses of the effects of CAR-T cell therapy on endogenous antitumor immune responses and efficacy of combined therapies.
source: Moreover, such syngeneic models enable analyses of the effects of CAR-T cell therapy on endogenous antitumor immune responses and efficacy of combined therapies that are limited in xenogeneic mouse models due to their incompetent host immunity and graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) by the xenografted T cells (Yaguchi et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation and logical inference about the advantages of syngeneic models.

claim: GPC1 is a cell-surface heparansulphate proteoglycan expressed in normal fetal tissues and tumor cells.
source: Glypican-1 (GPC1) is a cell-surface heparansulphate proteoglycan expressed in normal fetal tissues and tumor cells.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPC1 structure and expression pattern.

claim: A major function of GPC1 is its involvement in the development of brain in fetal phase.
source: A major function of GPC1 is its involvement in the development of brain in fetal phase.
evidence: This is established knowledge about GPC1 function, supported by the subsequent citation to Jen et al., 2009.

claim: Knockout of GPC1 exhibits no abnormalities in morphology, behavior, or life span in adult mice.
source: While knockout of GPC1 exhibits no abnormalities in morphology, behavior, or life span in adult mice, reduction in brain volume has been reported in early fetal phase (Jen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jen et al., 2009.

claim: Reduction in brain volume has been reported in early fetal phase in GPC1 knockout mice.
source: While knockout of GPC1 exhibits no abnormalities in morphology, behavior, or life span in adult mice, reduction in brain volume has been reported in early fetal phase (Jen et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Jen et al., 2009.

claim: GPC1 seems to have no critical function in healthy adult stage.
source: Thus, GPC1 seems to have no critical function in healthy adult stage.
evidence: This is inferred from the knockout data showing no abnormalities in adult mice.

claim: GPC1 is overexpressed in various human cancers including glioma, mesothelioma, several squamous cell carcinomas such as esophageal and cervical cancers, and several adenocarcinomas such as breast and pancreatic cancer.
source: Recently, we and other groups have reported the overexpression of GPC1 in various human cancers including glioma, mesothelioma, several squamous cell carcinomas (SCC) such as esophageal and cervical cancers, and several adenocarcinomas such as breast and pancreatic cancer (Hara et al., 2016; Matsuzaki et al., 2018; Matsuda et al., 2001; Melo et al., 2015; Duan et al., 2013; Su et al., 2006; Amatya et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: GPC1 expression in cancer is linked with malignant phenotypes such as promotion of cell-cycle and enhanced metastatic potential.
source: GPC1 expression in cancer is linked with malignant phenotypes such as promotion of cell-cycle and enhanced metastatic potential, and is considered as a prognostic factor in some cancers (Kleeff et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kleeff et al., 1998.

claim: GPC1 is considered as a prognostic factor in some cancers.
source: GPC1 expression in cancer is linked with malignant phenotypes such as promotion of cell-cycle and enhanced metastatic potential, and is considered as a prognostic factor in some cancers (Kleeff et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kleeff et al., 1998.

claim: Anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1-12) recognized both human and mouse GPC1.
source: In order to develop a cancer therapy targeting GPC1, we have previously generated anti-GPC1 cytotoxic monoclonal antibodies (mAb) (clone: 1–12). This anti-GPC1 mAb recognized both human and mouse GPC1, and inhibited the growth of GPC1-expressing human esophageal SCC xenografted in immunodeficient mice without any obvious adverse effects (Harada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Harada et al., 2017) and confirmed by SPR analysis data in the current manuscript.

claim: Anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1-12) inhibited the growth of GPC1-expressing human esophageal SCC xenografted in immunodeficient mice without any obvious adverse effects.
source: This anti-GPC1 mAb recognized both human and mouse GPC1, and inhibited the growth of GPC1-expressing human esophageal SCC xenografted in immunodeficient mice without any obvious adverse effects (Harada et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work (Harada et al., 2017).

claim: Most cervical squamous cell carcinoma tissues expressed higher hGPC1 mRNA than corresponding normal cervix tissues and various normal tissues.
source: Most of the cervical squamous cell carcinoma tissues expressed higher hGPC1 mRNA than corresponding normal cervix tissues and various normal tissues (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Normal tissues showed low to no expression of GPC1 when stained with anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1-12) compared to high expression in human esophageal carcinoma.
source: Compared to its high expression in human esophageal carcinoma, normal tissues showed low to no expression of GPC1 when stained with anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1–12).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The LH form of scFv showed high binding affinity against recombinant hGPC1 protein with KD value 9.06 × 10−9 M.
source: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis showed high binding affinity of LH or HL forms of scFv against recombinant hGPC1 protein as calculated KD value 9.06 × 10−9 M or 1.22 × 10−8 M, respectively, which was as high as that of anti-CD19 scFv currently used in clinical settings (Ghorashian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by SPR analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The HL form of scFv showed high binding affinity against recombinant hGPC1 protein with KD value 1.22 × 10−8 M.
source: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis showed high binding affinity of LH or HL forms of scFv against recombinant hGPC1 protein as calculated KD value 9.06 × 10−9 M or 1.22 × 10−8 M, respectively, which was as high as that of anti-CD19 scFv currently used in clinical settings (Ghorashian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by SPR analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The binding affinity of the generated scFv was as high as that of anti-CD19 scFv currently used in clinical settings.
source: Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) analysis showed high binding affinity of LH or HL forms of scFv against recombinant hGPC1 protein as calculated KD value 9.06 × 10−9 M or 1.22 × 10−8 M, respectively, which was as high as that of anti-CD19 scFv currently used in clinical settings (Ghorashian et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with cited clinical data (Ghorashian et al., 2019).

claim: GPC1-specific hCAR-T cells secreted IFNγ in a hGPC1-dependent manner when co-cultured with tumor cells.
source: When GPC1-specific hCAR-T cells were co-cultured with LK2-hGPC1 (a hGPC1 overexpressing lung carcinoma cell line), TE14 (an esophageal carcinoma cell line with endogenous hGPC1), or LK2-mock (a hGPC1-negative lung carcinoma cell line), IFNγ secretion and Cr51 release were detected in hGPC1-dependent manner (Figure 2B,C and D).
evidence: This is supported by IFNγ-releasing assay data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: GPC1-specific hCAR-T cells showed Cr51 release in a hGPC1-dependent manner when co-cultured with tumor cells.
source: When GPC1-specific hCAR-T cells were co-cultured with LK2-hGPC1 (a hGPC1 overexpressing lung carcinoma cell line), TE14 (an esophageal carcinoma cell line with endogenous hGPC1), or LK2-mock (a hGPC1-negative lung carcinoma cell line), IFNγ secretion and Cr51 release were detected in hGPC1-dependent manner (Figure 2B,C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Cr51 releasing assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The HL form of CAR possessed stronger antitumor activity than the LH form.
source: Our results also indicated that the HL form of CAR possessed stronger antitumor activity than the LH form.
evidence: This is inferred from the data shown in Figure 2C and D comparing LH and HL forms.

claim: hCAR-T cells effectively inhibited tumor growth in TE14 xenografted NOG mice compared to hCont-T cells.
source: The hCAR-T cells effectively inhibited tumor growth, compared to hCont-T cells (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumor growth data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: All NOG mice treated with hCAR-T cells suffered from and died of severe GVHD.
source: Due to administration of xenogeneic T cells, all NOG mice treated with hCAR-T cells suffered from and died of severe GVHD.
evidence: This is an observation from the xenogeneic model experiments.

claim: It was difficult to evaluate on-target off-tumor adverse effect in xenogeneic model due to GVHD.
source: Consequently, it was difficult to evaluate on-target off-tumor adverse effect in xenogeneic model.
evidence: This is inferred from the GVHD complications observed in the xenogeneic model.

claim: Heart, lung, and brain of mouse showed relatively high expression of Gpc1 mRNA compared to other tissues.
source: Similar to human tissues, heart, lung, and brain of mouse showed relatively high expression of Gpc1 mRNA (Figures 1A and 3A).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1-12) detected very low to no expression of GPC1 in normal tissues of adult mouse.
source: Similar to the observation in human adult tissues, anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1–12) detected very low to no expression of GPC1 in normal tissues of adult mouse (Figure 1C and Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: GPC1 shows similar expression pattern between human and mice at mRNA and protein levels.
source: These results indicated similar expression pattern of GPC1 between human and mice at mRNA and protein levels and suggested that syngeneic mouse model (C57BL/6) could be used for the evaluation of on-target off-tumor adverse effects.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparative data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: The LH form of scFv showed high binding affinity against mGPC1 with KD 5.18 × 10−8 M.
source: To generate GPC1-specific CAR-T cells from murine T cells and evaluate antitumor effects and adverse effects on normal tissues in syngeneic mouse models, we evaluated binding affinity of both LH and HL forms of scFv against recombinant mGPC1 protein by SPR analysis, and found that both LH (KD5.18 × 10−8 M) and HL (KD1.09 × 10−7 M) forms of scFv showed high binding affinity against mGPC1, although less affinity than those against hGPC1.
evidence: This is supported by SPR analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The HL form of scFv showed high binding affinity against mGPC1 with KD 1.09 × 10−7 M.
source: To generate GPC1-specific CAR-T cells from murine T cells and evaluate antitumor effects and adverse effects on normal tissues in syngeneic mouse models, we evaluated binding affinity of both LH and HL forms of scFv against recombinant mGPC1 protein by SPR analysis, and found that both LH (KD5.18 × 10−8 M) and HL (KD1.09 × 10−7 M) forms of scFv showed high binding affinity against mGPC1, although less affinity than those against hGPC1.
evidence: This is supported by SPR analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Both LH and HL forms of scFv showed less affinity for mGPC1 than for hGPC1.
source: To generate GPC1-specific CAR-T cells from murine T cells and evaluate antitumor effects and adverse effects on normal tissues in syngeneic mouse models, we evaluated binding affinity of both LH and HL forms of scFv against recombinant mGPC1 protein by SPR analysis, and found that both LH (KD5.18 × 10−8 M) and HL (KD1.09 × 10−7 M) forms of scFv showed high binding affinity against mGPC1, although less affinity than those against hGPC1.
evidence: This is supported by comparison of SPR analysis data for hGPC1 and mGPC1.

claim: The HL form of hCAR-T cells showed higher antitumor activity in vitro than the LH form.
source: The HL form was used for generating GPC1-specific mCAR-T cells, because the HL form of hCAR-T cells showed higher antitumor activity in vitro (Figure 2C and D).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro assay data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: GPC1-specific mCAR-T cells showed antigen-specific cytokine secretion when co-cultured with MC38-mGPC1 in vitro.
source: Cytokine secretion assay and cytotoxic assay were performed by co-culturing mCAR-T cells with MC38-mGPC1 in vitro. In these assays, we observed antigen-specific cytokine secretion and killing activity of GPC1-specific mCAR-T cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by cytokine secretion assay data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: GPC1-specific mCAR-T cells showed antigen-specific killing activity when co-cultured with MC38-mGPC1 in vitro.
source: Cytokine secretion assay and cytotoxic assay were performed by co-culturing mCAR-T cells with MC38-mGPC1 in vitro. In these assays, we observed antigen-specific cytokine secretion and killing activity of GPC1-specific mCAR-T cells (Figure 4C and D).
evidence: This is supported by Cr51 releasing assay data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: mCAR-T cells showed robust antitumor effects against established solid tumors without any obvious adverse effects.
source: Robust antitumor effects by mCAR-T cells against the established solid tumors were observed without any obvious adverse effects.
evidence: This is supported by in vivo tumor growth data in Figures 4E, 4F, and 4G, and safety data in Figure 5.

claim: mCAR-T cells were effective in inhibiting MC38-mGPC1 tumor growth compared to mCont-T cells.
source: In the MC38-mGPC1 mouse model, mCAR-T cells were effective in inhibiting tumor growth compared to mCont-T cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Four out of five mice receiving mCAR-T cells showed complete tumor eradication lasting at least 100 days in the MCA205-mGPC1 mouse model.
source: In the MCA205-mGPC1 mouse model, four out of the five mice receiving the mCAR-T cells showed complete tumor eradication lasting at least 100 days (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: mCAR-T cells showed significant in vivo antitumor activity against large MCA205-mGPC1 tumors (tumor volume >100 mm3) without any obvious adverse effects.
source: The mCAR-T cells were also injected into mice bearing large MCA205-mGPC1 tumor (tumor volume >100 mm3) and significant in vivo antitumor activity was observed without any obvious adverse effects (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Injected mCAR-T cells persisted in the peripheral blood and infiltrated into the tumor in MC38-mGPC1-bearing mice 15 days after administration.
source: Further, we confirmed that the injected mCAR-T cells persisted in the peripheral blood and infiltrated into the tumor in MC38-mGPC1-bearing mice 15 days after the administration (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: mCAR-T cells were present in the peripheral blood for over 60 days in MCA205-mGPC1 mice that resulted in complete eradication of tumors.
source: In the MCA205-mGPC1 mice that resulted in complete eradication of the tumors, we found that the mCAR-T cells were present in the peripheral blood for over 60 days (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated as an observation from the experiments, though data is not shown.

claim: mCAR-T cells in both circulation and tumor retained GPC1-specific IFNγ producing activity for at least 15 days.
source: 15 days after the mCAR-T cell injection, CD8+ T cells were collected from the spleens and tumor tissues of MC38-mGPC1-bearing mice and co-cultured with LK2-hGPC1 or LK2-mock. The results indicated that the mCAR-T cells in both circulation and tumor retained GPC1-specific IFNγ producing activity for at least 15 days (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by ex vivo cytokine secretion assay data shown in Figure 4I.

claim: gp70-specific IFNγ production was significantly enhanced by the administration of mCAR-T cells.
source: For this, CD8+ TIL were harvested from the tumor of MC38-mGPC1-bearing mice and re-stimulated in vitro with gp70, an epitope peptide of MC38 for induction of gp70-specific T cell response. As shown in Figure 4J, gp70-specific IFNγ production was significantly enhanced by the administration of mCAR-T cells.
evidence: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4J.

claim: Mice that had complete tumor eradication by mCAR-T cell therapy in the MCA205-mGPC1 model showed significant growth inhibition of re-challenged mGPC1-negative parental MCA205 tumors.
source: Moreover, to evaluate the presence and importance of endogenous T cell responses in vivo, mGPC1-negative parental MCA205 tumor cells were re-challenged into the mice which had complete tumor eradication by mCAR-T cell therapy in the MCA205-mGPC1 model (Figure 4F). These mice showed a significant growth inhibition of the inoculated mGPC1-negative tumors, indicating the induction and involvement of T cells specific for endogenous tumor antigens in the strong antitumor effects of GPC1-specific CAR-T cell therapy in the syngeneic tumor modes (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is supported by tumor re-challenge data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: The re-challenge experiment indicates the induction and involvement of T cells specific for endogenous tumor antigens in the strong antitumor effects of GPC1-specific CAR-T cell therapy.
source: These mice showed a significant growth inhibition of the inoculated mGPC1-negative tumors, indicating the induction and involvement of T cells specific for endogenous tumor antigens in the strong antitumor effects of GPC1-specific CAR-T cell therapy in the syngeneic tumor modes (Figure 4K).
evidence: This is inferred from the tumor re-challenge data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: No significant difference was observed in body weights of mice treated with either mCAR-T cells or mCont-T cells.
source: No significant difference was observed in body weights of mice treated with either mCAR-T cells or mCont-T cells (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by body weight data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: No differences of gross appearance or behavior were observed between mice treated with mCAR-T cells and control mice.
source: Similarly, no differences of gross appearance or behavior were observed between the treated and control mice.
evidence: This is an observation from the in vivo experiments.

claim: No obvious tissue damage or infiltration of mCAR-T cells was observed in any of tested organs including the heart and brain.
source: Histologically, no obvious tissue damage or infiltration of mCAR-T cells was observed in any of tested organs including the heart and brain that showed detectable expression of GPC1 mRNA by qPCR (Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is supported by histological data shown in Figure 5B and supplementary figures.

claim: Administration of more than 10 times higher numbers of CAR-T cells did not show obvious adverse effects with significant antitumor effects against larger tumor.
source: Furthermore, administration of more than 10 times higher numbers of CAR-T cells did not show obvious adverse effects (data not shown) with significant antitumor effects against larger tumor (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by the high-dose experiment data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Most of mCAR-T cells and endogenous T cells in tumor tissues expressed PD-1 in the MC38-mGPC1 mouse model.
source: In MC38-mGPC1 mouse model, most of mCAR-T cells and endogenous T cells in tumor tissues expressed PD-1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The frequency of PD-1 expression on mCAR-T cells tended to be higher than that on mCont-T cells, although it did not show significance.
source: The frequency of PD-1 expression on mCAR-T cells tended to be higher than that on mCont-T cells, although it did not show significance.
evidence: This is inferred from the flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: MC38-mGPC1 stably expressed PD-L1.
source: As MC38-mGPC1 stably expressed PD-L1, we assessed whether anti-PD-1 Ab could enhance antitumor activities of the mCAR-T cell therapy (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated as an observation that motivated the combination therapy experiment.

claim: The combination therapy of mCAR-T cells and anti-PD-1 Ab resulted in stronger antitumor activity than that of the mCAR-T cells alone.
source: The combination therapy of mCAR-T cells and anti-PD-1 Ab resulted in stronger antitumor activity than that of the mCAR-T cells alone (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by tumor growth data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Two out of five mice receiving the combination therapy showed complete tumor eradication.
source: While the mice treated with either anti-PD1 Ab or mCAR-T cells alone showed partial inhibition of tumor growth, two out of the five mice receiving the combination therapy showed complete tumor eradication (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by individual tumor growth curves shown in Figure 6D.

claim: None of the mice in the combination therapy experiment seemed to display any adverse effects with clinical symptoms.
source: In addition, none of the mice in this experiment seemed to display any adverse effects with clinical symptoms.
evidence: This is an observation from the combination therapy experiment.

claim: Antitumor effects of anti-PD-1 Ab were relatively weak due to preconditioning with total body irradiation for in vivo CAR-T cell expansion.
source: Antitumor effects of anti-PD-1 Ab were relatively weak due to preconditioning with total body irradiation for in vivo CAR-T cell expansion.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental design and observed results.

claim: Immunogenicity of the chicken-based CAR-T cells may cause rejection of the CAR-T cells and poor responses in patients.
source: Immunogenicity of the chicken-based CAR-T cells may cause rejection of the CAR-T cells and poor responses in patients.
evidence: This is speculation about potential clinical limitations.

claim: Non-humanized CD19-specific CAR-T cells have demonstrated significant antitumor effects for a variety of B cell malignancy possibly due to their relatively immunosuppressed condition via malignancy and chemotherapy/preconditioning.
source: However, non-humanized CD19-specific CAR-T cells have demonstrated significant antitumor effects for a variety of B cell malignancy possibly due to their relatively immunosuppressed condition via malignancy and chemotherapy/preconditioning.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from clinical trials of CD19 CAR-T cells.

claim: The chicken-based GPC1-specific CAR-T cells showed strong antitumor effects in this study.
source: And the chicken-based GPC1-specific CAR-T cells showed strong antitumor effects in this study.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Some normal tissues showed slight staining by the commercial polyclonal anti-GPC1 Ab in IHC.
source: On the other hand, we detected low expression of hGPC1 mRNA in all tested normal tissues and we also previously reported that some normal tissues showed slight staining by the commercial polyclonal anti-GPC1 Ab in IHC.
evidence: This is based on previous observations cited in the discussion.

claim: Human esophageal SCC tissues showed strong and broad expression of GPC1 by IHC using anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1-12).
source: In this study, we evaluated hGPC1 protein expressions by IHC using our anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1–12) and found that GPC1 expression was under the detection sensitivity in human normal tissues, whereas human esophageal SCC tissues showed strong and broad expression.
evidence: This is supported by IHC data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The difference in IHC results of commercial polyclonal Ab and anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1-12) might be related to the difference of epitopes recognized by the antibodies.
source: The difference in IHC results of commercial polyclonal Ab and our anti-GPC1 mAb might be related to the difference of epitopes recognized by the antibodies.
evidence: This is speculation about the reason for different IHC results.

claim: Anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1-12) specifically recognizes GPC1 protein expressed on tumor cells and is suitable for the generation of CAR-T cells.
source: Although it is still uncertain whether GPC1 protein expression is completely negative in normal tissues of human, our anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1–12) specifically recognizes GPC1 protein expressed on tumor cells and is suitable for the generation of CAR-T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the IHC data and functional CAR-T cell data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A major mechanism of on-target off-tumor adverse effects is thought to be the recognition of target antigens expressed in normal cells by CAR-T cells.
source: A major mechanism of on-target off-tumor adverse effects is thought to be the recognition of target antigens expressed in normal cells by CAR-T cells (Tran et al., 2013; Lamers et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Some CAR-T cell therapies in clinical trials are targeting antigens that are expressed in both tumor and normal tissues and are demonstrating favorable responses without obvious adverse effects.
source: However, some CAR-T cell therapies in clinical trials are targeting antigens that are expressed in both tumor and normal tissues (e.g. mesothelin, GD2, and IL13Rα2) and are demonstrating favorable responses without obvious adverse effects (Beatty et al., 2014; Brown et al., 2016; Rossig et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial reports.

claim: Mesothelin is broadly expressed on mesothelial cells at protein levels.
source: For example, although mesothelin is broadly expressed on mesothelial cells at protein levels, patients treated with mesothelin-specific CAR-T cells show objective antitumor responses (Beatty et al., 2014; Morello et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Patients treated with mesothelin-specific CAR-T cells show objective antitumor responses.
source: For example, although mesothelin is broadly expressed on mesothelial cells at protein levels, patients treated with mesothelin-specific CAR-T cells show objective antitumor responses (Beatty et al., 2014; Morello et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Tumor-specific killing by GPC1-specific CAR-T cells may be explained by a tumor-specific recognition by the anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1-12).
source: In our study, tumor-specific killing by our CAR-T cells may be explained by a tumor-specific recognition by the anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1–12).
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of tumor-specific killing.

claim: Even if GPC1 is expressed on some normal tissues and can be recognized by anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1-12), its expression might be too low to activate GPC1-specific CAR-T cells.
source: Another possibility may be that, even if GPC1 is expressed on some normal tissues and can be recognized by anti-GPC1 mAb (clone: 1–12), its expression might be too low to activate GPC1-specific CAR-T cells.
evidence: This is speculation about why no adverse effects were observed.

claim: GPC1-specific human or murine CAR-T cells did not respond to LK2-mock or MC38-mock tumor cells.
source: Indeed, our GPC1-specific human or murine CAR-T cells did not respond to LK2-mock or MC38-mock tumor cells (Figures 2C, D, 4C and D), although LK2-mock weakly expressed hGPC1 mRNA (hGPC1/GAPDH; 0.00059) at similar level to the normal cervix tissues (hGPC1/GAPDH; mean 0.00209 ± 0.00185, range 0.00065–0.00473) and MC38-mock expressed weak mGpc1 mRNA (mGpc1/Gapdh; 0.00532) at similar level to the evaluated various normal tissues (mGpc1/Gapdh; mean 0.02284 ± 0.01684, range 0.00341–0.06406) without detectable GPC1 protein (Figures 1, 2B and 3).
evidence: This is supported by functional assay data shown in Figures 2C, D, 4C and D.

claim: CAR-T cells have thresholds of antigen density required to induce responses against target antigens.
source: In addition, some reports demonstrated that CAR-T cells have thresholds of antigen density required to induce responses against target antigens (James et al., 2010; James et al., 2008; Walker et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The lack of adverse effects may be explained by the existence of anatomical barriers or deficiency of chemokines for the attraction of T cells into normal tissues.
source: Other possible explanation is the existence of anatomical barriers or deficiency of chemokines for the attraction of T cells into normal tissues (Beatty et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: VEGFR2-specific CAR-T cells exhibited effective antitumor activity without any adverse effects in syngeneic mouse models.
source: Rosenberg et al. reported the use of syngeneic mouse models for the evaluation of CAR-T cells targeting VEGFR2 and FAP expressed in the stromal cells in tumor microenvironment rather than the tumor cells themselves (Chinnasamy et al., 2010; Tran et al., 2013). Although VEGFR2-specific CAR-T cells exhibited effective antitumor activity without any adverse effects, FAP-specific CAR-T cells resulted in lethal bone toxicities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by Rosenberg et al.

claim: FAP-specific CAR-T cells resulted in lethal bone toxicities in syngeneic mouse models.
source: Although VEGFR2-specific CAR-T cells exhibited effective antitumor activity without any adverse effects, FAP-specific CAR-T cells resulted in lethal bone toxicities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by Rosenberg et al.

claim: The findings from VEGFR2 and FAP CAR-T cell studies suggested the benefits of utilizing syngeneic mouse models for assessing the possible adverse effects of CAR-T cells.
source: These findings suggested the benefits of utilizing syngeneic mouse models for assessing the possible adverse effects of CAR-T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the contrasting outcomes of VEGFR2 and FAP CAR-T cell studies.

claim: CAR-T cells enhanced the CTL induction and generated immunological memory against non-GPC1 endogenous tumor antigens.
source: We demonstrated that CAR-T cells enhanced the CTL induction and generated immunological memory against non-GPC1 endogenous tumor antigens.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figures 4J and 4K showing enhanced gp70-specific responses and tumor rejection upon re-challenge.

claim: The enhanced CTL induction and immunological memory might explain stronger antitumor effects of mCAR-T cells in the immunocompetent syngeneic mouse models compared to the delayed antitumor effects of hCAR-T cells in the immunodeficient xenogeneic mouse model.
source: These findings might explain stronger antitumor effects of mCAR-T cells in the immunocompetent syngeneic mouse models compared to the delayed antitumor effects of hCAR-T cells in the immunodeficient xenogeneic mouse model.
evidence: This is inferred from comparing the results in syngeneic and xenogeneic models.

claim: Lysis of tumor cells and secretion of multiple cytokines by CAR-T cells created an optimal environment for the activation of dendritic cells and CTL.
source: We speculated that lysis of tumor cells and secretion of multiple cytokines by CAR-T cells created an optimal environment for the activation of dendritic cells and CTL.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of antigen spreading.

claim: Induction of antitumor antibodies against novel antigens was reported in clinical trials of mesothelin-specific CAR-T cells.
source: Such kinds of phenomena were actually reported in some clinical trials. For example, induction of antitumor antibodies against novel antigens was reported in clinical trials of mesothelin-specific CAR-T cells (Beatty et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a clinical trial report.

claim: Development of adaptive immunity against a broad spectrum of tumor-specific antigens by antigen spread is an important secondary mechanism underlying the potency of immunotherapy.
source: Development of adaptive immunity against a broad spectrum of tumor-specific antigens by antigen spread is an important secondary mechanism underlying the potency of immunotherapy, which could overcome immune escape of the CAR-T cell therapy targeting single antigen (Galon and Bruni, 2019; Kato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Antigen spread could overcome immune escape of the CAR-T cell therapy targeting single antigen.
source: Development of adaptive immunity against a broad spectrum of tumor-specific antigens by antigen spread is an important secondary mechanism underlying the potency of immunotherapy, which could overcome immune escape of the CAR-T cell therapy targeting single antigen (Galon and Bruni, 2019; Kato et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Delayed antitumor effects observed in the NOG mouse model compared to syngeneic mouse models might be explained by xenogeneic GVHD reaction that might promote late activation and expansion of hCAR-T cells.
source: For example, delayed antitumor effects observed in the NOG mouse model (Figure 2E) compared to syngeneic mouse models (Figures 4E, F and G) might be explained by xenogeneic GVHD reaction that might promote late activation and expansion of hCAR-T cells.
evidence: This is speculation based on comparing results from different model systems.

claim: Strong PD-1 expression on the administered CAR-T cells and endogenous TIL suggested occurrence of T cell activation and exhaustion.
source: In the syngeneic mouse models, strong PD-1 expression on the administered CAR-T cells and endogenous TIL, which suggested occurrence of T cell activation and exhaustion (Iwai et al., 2017), prompted us to evaluate synergistic effects of CAR-T cells and anti-PD-1 Ab therapies in our syngeneic mouse model.
evidence: This is inferred from the PD-1 expression data and supported by citation.

claim: The synergistic effect of combination therapy may be explained by enhanced effector function of administered CAR-T cells and endogenous antitumor CTL by anti-PD-1 Ab.
source: This synergistic effect may be explained by enhanced effector function of administered CAR-T cells and endogenous antitumor CTL by anti-PD-1 Ab.
evidence: This is speculation about the mechanism of synergy.

claim: PD-1 is reported to be involved in the suppression of CD28/B7 signal.
source: In addition, as PD-1 is reported to be involved in the suppression of CD28/B7 signal, it might be also possible that the anti-PD-1 Ab recovered the suppressed CD28 signal from dendritic cells during the T cell priming phase and consequently led to enhanced CTL induction (Hui et al., 2017; Kamphorst et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Anti-PD-1 Ab might recover the suppressed CD28 signal from dendritic cells during the T cell priming phase and consequently lead to enhanced CTL induction.
source: In addition, as PD-1 is reported to be involved in the suppression of CD28/B7 signal, it might be also possible that the anti-PD-1 Ab recovered the suppressed CD28 signal from dendritic cells during the T cell priming phase and consequently led to enhanced CTL induction (Hui et al., 2017; Kamphorst et al., 2017).

claim: High frequency of PD-1 expression on CAR-T cells was associated with treatment failure in human clinical trials.

evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial reports.

claim: Upregulation of PD-L1 expression on tumor cells after infusion of CAR-T cells was observed in non-responder patients in clinical trials of EGFRvIII-specific CAR-T cells for glioma.
source: In the clinical trials of EGFRvIII-specific CAR-T cells for glioma patients, upregulation of PD-L1 expression on tumor cells after infusion of CAR-T cells was observed in non-responder patients.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from clinical trials.

claim: PD-1 is a potential target to improve the efficacy of CAR-T cell therapies.
source: These reports suggest that PD-1 is a potential target to improve the efficacy of CAR-T cell therapies and syngeneic mouse models are effective tools to evaluate the effectiveness of combination therapy with CAR-T cells.
evidence: This is inferred from clinical trial data and the current study's findings.

claim: Syngeneic mouse models are effective tools to evaluate the effectiveness of combination therapy with CAR-T cells.
